steps.intro: Listen for the quick “e” of the shewa, and for the throat letters א ה ח ע.

cards.title: The shewa ְ: a quick e, or nothing
body: Two dots one above the other under a letter are a shewa. Sometimes you say it as a very short e; sometimes it is silent and just shows the letter has no vowel.

Said: at the start of a word, as in דְּבָרִים, de-va-RIM. Silent: at the end of a syllable, as in מִדְבָּר, mid-BAR. When two shewas stand side by side in the middle of a word, the first is silent and the second is said. A shewa is also said under a doubled letter, and after a long vowel: יָלְדָה, ya-le-DAH, “she bore”.

examples.en: words: the shewa starts the word, so say it
wilderness: the shewa closes “mid”, so it's silent

cards.title: The throat letters: א ה ח ע
body: These letters are made at the back of the throat, and it shows in the spelling. They never take a plain said shewa: instead they take a shewa with a short vowel beside it, ֲ ֱ ֳ (a, e, o). Grammar books call these hateph vowels.
They like the a-vowels: where מֶלֶךְ has two e's, נַעַר (young man), with ע in the middle, has two a's.
And they can't be doubled, so they never take the doubling dot. ר refuses the doubling dot too, though it takes an ordinary shewa. Lesson 7 shows what happens when “the” would double one.

cards.title: A sneaky a, and letters that go quiet
body: When ח or ע ends a word after any vowel except an a-vowel, a patah is slipped in under it and said first: רוּחַ is RU-ach, not ru-cha. This is called a furtive patah.
א at the end of a syllable makes no sound: לֹא is just lo. ה at the end of a word is usually silent too, as in תּוֹרָה, to-RAH.

examples.en: say the a before the ch

cards.prompt: In מִדְבָּר (wilderness), the shewa under ד is…
options: silent: it closes the syllable mid
cards.explain: It ends the syllable mid, so it is silent: mid-BAR.

cards.prompt: In דְּבָרִים (words), the first shewa is…
cards.explain: A shewa at the start of a word is always said: de-va-RIM.

cards.prompt: Match each hateph vowel to its sound.
Why does אֲנִי (I) have ֲ and not a plain shewa ְ?
options: א is a throat letter, and they take the hateph vowels
It is the first word of a sentence
cards.explain: Throat letters can't carry a plain said shewa, so they take ֲ, ֱ or ֳ instead.
A furtive patah is said before its letter: RU-ach.

steps.intro: Look for shewas, said and silent, and the throat letters with their hateph vowels.

cards.note: Near the end, וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים: “and the Spirit of God”. רוּחַ has its furtive patah, and אֱלֹהִים starts with hateph segol.
The last word is אֱמֶת, truth: “and your law is truth”.

source.book: Wegner, A Simplified Grammar of Biblical Hebrew
source.chapter: Lessons 3 and 5: Quiescent and Guttural Letters; Simple and Compound Shewas

grammarCheck.verdict: agrees, two wordings fixed; 18 Nov 2026 wording corrections (see claims marked 18 Nov); 18 Nov 2026 second-review corrections; 19 Nov 2026: corrected sentences re-read against Wegner lessons 3 and 5, all agree

claims.claim: shewa is said at the start of a word, silent when it closes a syllable; of two in a row the first is silent, the second said
throat letters take hateph vowels instead of a said shewa, prefer a-vowels and are never doubled
a furtive patah comes under a final ח or ע after another vowel
claims.note: Wegner: after a long vowel; the data also has it after qibbuts (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ) and never after qamets or patah, so the lesson says 'after any vowel except an a-vowel'

claims.claim: רוּחַ shown as two syllables (drill label 'Syllables')
claims.note: Wegner: one syllable; the drill now asks how it is said

claims.claim: א at the end of a syllable and ה at the end of a word are silent
a shewa is also said under a doubled letter and after a long vowel (יָלְדָה ya-le-DAH)
claims.note: 18 Nov 2026: added so the lesson matches what Listen says; GKC §10 c and l; Wegner lesson 5 agrees (re-read 19 Nov)

claims.claim: throat letters like a-vowels: נַעַר has two a's where מֶלֶךְ has two e's
claims.note: 18 Nov 2026: had 'patah under both throat letters', but נ isn't one and ר has no vowel; re-read against Wegner lessons 3 and 5 on 19 Nov 2026: agrees

claims.claim: ר is not a throat letter: it takes an ordinary shewa, but refuses the doubling dot
claims.note: 18 Nov 2026 (second review): title had '(and ר)'; GKC §22; re-read against Wegner lessons 3 and 5 on 19 Nov 2026: agrees

claims.claim: a shewa after a long vowel is said, whether or not that vowel is stressed (יָלְדָה ya-le-DAH)
claims.note: 19 Nov 2026: Wegner lesson 5 lists 'follow a long vowel' (יֵלְכוּ yē-le-ḵû) among the said shewas and makes no exception for a stressed vowel; the app's exceptions (a closed syllable: final pair of letters, the -nâ ending, a pausal qamets for patah such as לָ֑יְלָה) follow GKC §10 and are beyond the lesson

claims.claim: a guttural closing a syllable can carry a silent shewa (יָדַעְתִּי)
claims.note: 19 Nov 2026: Wegner lesson 3; the lesson says throat letters never take a said shewa, which is the same rule
